Why Slow Bread Tastes Better

By Ada Baker on 14 March 2025

Share on X Share on Facebook

Most home bakers rush the dough. They mix, knead, prove for an hour, and bake. The bread is fine. But a long fermentation makes bread that tastes deeper, keeps longer, and digests more easily.

In this article I explain what happens inside the dough during a slow rise, and how you can use the fridge to get the same result with little extra work. I tested each method over three months with the same flour, water and salt.

What happens during a slow rise

Yeast and bacteria break starches into sugars. The sugars feed the yeast. Over many hours, bacteria also make lactic and acetic acids. These acids give flavour. Enzymes break proteins into amino acids, which brown in the oven and give a darker crust.

Short rises do not give the enzymes enough time. The crumb is pale and the crust stays thin. A good rule is twelve hours or more at a cool temperature.

Using the fridge

The fridge slows the yeast more than the bacteria. So a cold rise builds more acid for the same amount of gas. Put the shaped loaf in the fridge overnight, then bake it straight from cold.

Shaped loaves resting at 4 °C.

Timing table

Bulk rise4 h22 °C

A simple schedule

  1. Mix at 6 pm.
  2. Stretch and fold every 30 minutes for 2 hours.
  3. Shape at 10 pm and put it in the fridge.
  4. Bake at 7 am.
hydration = water / flour
# 375 g / 500 g = 75 %

Time is the cheapest ingredient in the bakery.
